title: Volume for Grade 5: Cubic Units, Cubes and Capacity + Free Quiz
meta_title: Volume Grade 5: Cube & Cuboid + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Volume grade 5 made simple: count unit cubes, use length by width by height, and tell volume from capacity. Free 8-question quiz plus printable worksheet.
excerpt: Volume is the first time a Grade 5 child measures space instead of length. Here is how to teach it with unit cubes, the length × width × height rule, and the volume-versus-capacity trap — plus a quick quiz to check it stuck.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Grade 5 child a small cardboard box and ask how much space is inside, and you will usually get an answer in centimetres — the length of one edge. That is the whole hurdle right there. Up to now they have measured length, a single straight line. Volume is different: it is the amount of space a solid takes up, and you cannot capture space with one number off a ruler. Sorting out that confusion is exactly what a good volume grade 5 lesson does, and it is easier than most parents expect once you reach for unit cubes instead of a formula.

In my experience teaching ten-year-olds, the children who struggle are almost always the ones who were handed ‘length × width × height’ on day one. The formula is the destination, not the starting point. Start with cubes you can hold.

Volume is measured in cubic units, not centimetres

A length is measured in centimetres (cm). An area is measured in square centimetres (cm²) — little squares that tile a flat surface. Volume needs a solid unit: the cubic centimetre (cm³), a tiny cube one centimetre along every edge. Bigger solids, like a room or a water tank, are measured in cubic metres (m³).

Getting a child to say ‘cubic centimetres’ out loud, and to picture a little cube rather than a flat square, is half the battle. I make them draw one small cube and label all three edges 1 cm before we go anywhere near a box.

Counting unit cubes: the method before the formula

Give a child some interlocking cubes (or sugar cubes, or dice) and build a cuboid. Now just count them. A block that is 4 cubes long, 3 cubes wide and 2 cubes high holds… well, count the bottom layer first: 4 × 3 = 12 cubes in one layer. There are 2 layers, so 24 cubes altogether. The volume is 24 cubic units.

Do this three or four times with different blocks and something clicks on its own: children start counting one layer and then multiplying by the number of layers, because counting all 24 by hand is tedious. That shortcut is the formula, discovered rather than dictated. It sticks far better this way.

Why layers matter

The layer idea rescues children who later meet a half-filled box or a shape with a missing corner. If they understand volume as ‘how many unit cubes fit inside’, they can reason about odd shapes. If they only know a formula, they freeze the moment the shape is not a perfect box.

The volume grade 5 formula: length × width × height

Once the counting makes sense, name the shortcut. For any cuboid:

  • Volume = length × width × height
  • For a cube, all three edges are equal, so volume = side × side × side.
  • The answer is always in cubic units — cm³ if the edges were in cm.

So a cuboid 5 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm has a volume of 5 × 3 × 2 = 30 cm³. A cube with a 4 cm edge has a volume of 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 cm³. Notice the order of multiplication does not change the answer — a useful reassurance for a child who multiplied the numbers in a different order and panicked.

Volume versus capacity: the trap worth spelling out

This is where marks quietly disappear in exams. Volume is the space a solid takes up, measured in cubic units. Capacity is how much a container can hold, usually measured in litres (l) and millilitres (ml). They describe the same box from two angles — one from the outside, one from the inside.

The bridge a Grade 5 child needs is a single fact: 1 millilitre fills exactly 1 cubic centimetre, and 1 litre = 1000 ml = 1000 cm³. So a tank measuring 10 cm × 10 cm × 10 cm has a volume of 1000 cm³ and a capacity of 1 litre. Teach that one worked example and the two ideas stop feeling like separate topics.

One honest caveat: do not overload the litre-to-cm³ conversion in the first week. Let counting cubes and the formula settle for a few days first. Rushing the conversion is the fastest way to muddle a child who was doing fine.

A simple week of practice

Ten focused minutes a day beats a marathon on Sunday. A rhythm that works: two days building and counting cubes, two days on the length × width × height rule with written questions, one day on the volume-versus-capacity link, and the weekend for mixed problems where the child has to decide which idea applies. That deciding step is where real understanding shows.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free, eight-question quiz covering exactly what we have gone through — cubic units, counting unit cubes, the cuboid formula, and volume versus capacity. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer graded practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives plenty of questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 5 Volume Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on cubic units, counting unit cubes, the cuboid formula and capacity. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 5 volume of cubes and cuboids

questions.q: Which unit is used to measure volume?
questions.explanation: Volume measures space in three directions, so it uses a solid unit — the cubic centimetre (cm3).

questions.q: A block is 2 cubes long, 2 cubes wide and 2 cubes high. How many unit cubes is that?
questions.explanation: One layer is 2 × 2 = 4 cubes, and there are 2 layers: 4 × 2 = 8 cubic units.

questions.q: What is the volume of a cuboid 5 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm?
What is the volume of a cube with a 4 cm edge?
questions.explanation: For a cube, volume = side × side × side = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 cm3.

questions.q: Which unit measures capacity — how much liquid a container can hold?
questions.explanation: Capacity is measured in litres and millilitres (ml). Volume uses cubic units like cm3.

questions.q: A box measures 6 cm by 2 cm by 2 cm. What is its volume?
A cuboid has a bottom layer of 12 unit cubes and is 3 layers tall. What is its volume?
questions.explanation: Multiply one layer by the number of layers: 12 × 3 = 36 cubic units.

questions.q: How many millilitres are in 1 litre?
questions.explanation: 1 litre = 1000 ml, which also equals 1000 cm3 of space.

faq.q: What does volume mean in Grade 5 maths?
faq.a: Volume is the amount of space a solid object takes up, measured in cubic units such as cubic centimetres (cm³). In Grade 5, children find the volume of cubes and cuboids by counting unit cubes and by using length × width × height.

faq.q: How do you find the volume of a cuboid?
faq.a: Multiply its three dimensions: volume = length × width × height. For example, a cuboid 5 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm has a volume of 5 × 3 × 2 = 30 cm³. The answer is always in cubic units.

faq.q: What is the difference between volume and capacity?
faq.a: Volume is the space a solid takes up, measured in cubic units like cm³. Capacity is how much a container can hold, measured in litres and millilitres. They link with one fact: 1 ml fills exactly 1 cm³, so 1 litre = 1000 cm³.

faq.q: Should children count cubes or use the formula first?
faq.a: Counting unit cubes first, every time. When a child builds a block and counts the layers, they discover length × width × height on their own, and it sticks far better than a formula handed over on day one.
